Chapter 4: Making Ideas Real with Concrete Details
You know, abstract ideas—they can be tough to wrap your head around, and honestly, they’re easy to forget. But when you want an idea to really stick, you’ve got to make it real. That means turning something fuzzy into something you can actually see, touch, or picture in your mind. When you add concrete details, you transform a vague concept into an experience you can almost feel.
Think about it—our minds are wired to remember what we can picture or experience. Let’s say someone talks about “improving education.” Pretty broad, right? But if you say, “Imagine a classroom where every child has their own book and a desk,” suddenly, you’re painting a scene. It’s clear. It’s memorable.
Here’s something worth paying attention to: when you’re sharing an idea with folks who don’t have the same background or expertise as you, concreteness is your best friend. Experts might throw around abstract terms because they’re comfortable with them, but most people need real examples to connect the dots.
Take this for example—“We need to reduce waste.” Ok, but what does that really mean? Now try, “Let’s cut down on the number of plastic bottles we use each week.” That’s specific. It’s something you can actually do, and you can tell if you’re making progress.
So, how do you make your ideas more concrete? Here are a few practical ways:
First, use sensory language. Talk about what people can see, hear, or touch.
Second, give specific examples. Bring in real-life scenarios or stories that make your point come alive.
And finally, skip the jargon. Swap out those technical words for everyday language that anyone can understand.
The cool thing about concreteness is that it helps your idea go the distance. When your message is tied to a vivid image or a specific moment, people remember it—and they’re more likely to share it with others. That’s why stories and anecdotes are so powerful. They’re packed with concrete details that just stick.
Picture this: A charity wants donations for clean water. They could list a bunch of statistics, but instead, they describe a village where kids walk miles every day to fetch water from a muddy stream. Suddenly, you can see the struggle—and it feels urgent and real.
So, here’s the key takeaway: if you want your ideas to be understood, remembered, and acted on, ground them in concrete details. It’s the glue that holds those big, abstract concepts together and makes them accessible to everyone.
